Distributed Multi-Armed Bandits for Slotted ALOHA Authors: Kamil Szczech , Maksymilian Wojnar , Krzysztof Rusek , Katarzyna Kosek-Szott , Szymon Szott View a PDF of the paper titled Can Bandits Learn to Share a Channel? Distributed Multi-Armed Bandits for Slotted ALOHA, by Kamil Szczech and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Slotted ALOHA networks constitute a playground for research on machine learning (ML)-based channel access schemes. We consider ML agents deployed in such networks and operating under severe constraints: fully distributed (independent operation), fully online (no pre-training), aperiodic (no fixed schedule), and with no explicit coordination (no signaling). We ask whether a multi-armed bandit (MAB), a minimal reinforcement learning agent, can learn the optimal policy for a capture-free slotted ALOHA system. We evaluate several MAB algorithms on aggregate network throughput and per-node fairness. Our best-performing agent is based on a Softmax bandit, which we call SALSA (Softmax ALOHA Learning for Shared Access). SALSA learns a per-node transmission policy close to optimal, with throughput near the theoretical maximum for fair random access. We achieve performance comparable to a competing state-of-the-art solution, but without requiring a priori knowledge of the network size. Abstract Multi-agent-based simulations (MABS) of electric vehicle (EV) home charging ecosystems generate large, complex, and stochastic time-series datasets that capture interactions between households, grid infrastructure, and energy markets. These interactions can lead to unexpected system-level events, such as transformer overloads or consumer dissatisfaction, that are difficult to detect and explain through static post-processing. This paper presents a modular, Python-based dashboard framework—built using Dash by Plotly—that enables efficient, multi-level exploration and root-cause analysis of emergent behavior in MABS outputs. The system features three coordinated views (System Overview, System Analysis, and Consumer Analysis), each offering high-resolution visualizations such as time-series plots, spatial heatmaps, and agent-specific drill-down tools. A case study simulating full EV adoption with smart charging in a Danish residential network demonstrates how the dashboard supports rapid identification and contextual explanation of anomalies, including clustered transformer overloads and time-dependent charging failures. The framework facilitates actionable insight generation for researchers and distribution system operators, and its architecture is adaptable to other distributed energy resources and complex energy systems. Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2611.21478 (cs) [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility Authors: Ruizhe Li , Licheng Zhang , Mingxuan Du , Zhendong Mao View a PDF of the paper titled Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility, by Ruizhe Li and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Whether a stored memory helps answer a user's question often depends on world knowledge rather than surface similarity. Jetriever replaces similarity search with full-pool utility scoring: given a query, it uses Jev, an LLM-derived System One decision model, to score every stored memory for the probability that it is useful to the answer, ranking the memory pool directly by those probabilities. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, Jetriever places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases (versus 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM with user-turn indexing) and reaches 76.0% end-to-end Application, compared with at most 16.0% across published retrieval and memory systems. A controlled 20-question comparison disentangles recognizing implicit evidence from ranking it properly: Jev and Qwen3.5-9B both recover 90% of gold exchanges within the top 50 (versus 30% for the BERT-based decision model Laya), yet at rank 1 Jev reaches 85% while Qwen3.5-9B drops to 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever raises the four-dimension average from 44.3% (ReFind) to 55.4%, at a mean retrieval cost of USD 0.00834 per InMind query and USD 0.03103 per MAB query. Together, these results show that effective utility retrieval hinges on combining broad world knowledge, calibrated ranking probabilities, and affordable full-pool evaluation. Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.23977 (cs) [Submitted on 18 Nov 2026] Title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks Authors: Langtian Qin , Avishkar Dnyaneshwar Kawadgave , Ian Andrew Harshbarger , Leïla Nasraoui , Carla Fabiana Chiasserini , Marco Levorato View a PDF of the paper titled OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks, by Langtian Qin and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.
